This bill strengthens how the social media minimum age framework is enforced.
It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers to demand documents and information from anyone relevant to compliance checks.
Civil penalties for breaking minimum age rules would double to 60,000 penalty units, worth about $99 million for a body corporate.
Expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to compel production of documents from any person.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 2, Part 4A from 30,000 to 60,000 penalty units.
Increases the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 4, Part 4A from 500 to 1,000 penalty units.
Providers of age-restricted social media platforms and the eSafety Commissioner are affected.

Tony Pasin I feel a little like an imposter talking on this bill. Many of my colleagues who know me know that I'm probably best described as a Luddite. Even as a Luddite, in this role one has to be across the role of online presences. In fact, I am wanted, recently, to describe myself to colleagues, members of the party and constituents otherwise as a 'content creator'. I've got to tell you, Mr Deputy Speaker, when I entered the parliament in 2013, if someone told me it was a condition of this role that I would have to become a digital content creator, I would have stayed in the law and transitioned to the farm. I wouldn't have sought preselection. I wouldn't have worked very hard to obtain that preselection and then worked very hard during the election of 2013 and subsequent elections since then. But the truth is that, in the modern age, if you want to share and communicate with your constituency, or if you're in business and you want to share and communicate with customers, if you're not on a digital platform then you're missing out. And young people have gained aptitude towards digital acumen faster than any other cohort in the country. I've got a 16-year-old and a 10-year-old, and their acumen around digital platforms and these things is just a sight to behold. I'm not one of those people who come in here and say that everything about online experiences is wrong. I don't conform to that view. Like everything, there need to be appropriate safeguards; there need to be appropriate barriers. That is what we're seeking to achieve here, and I of course support my colleague the member for Lindsay's amendment. But it is important that we understand that, as positive as experiences can be in the digital online environment, there are also substantial risks. Like others, I've read of very tragic circumstances. I've had constituents, parents, come to me concerned about the way algorithms are seeking to lock young people in. In other words, they voted in favour of a motion to agree with the main idea of the bill and can now discuss it in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd069), which is a document prepared by the parliamentary library: > *The Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026 (the Bill) would amend the Fair Work Act 2009 (FW Act) and related legislation to effect industrial relations changes. The key measures are:* > > * *Expanding powers of the Fair Work Commission (FWC) to deal with applications.* > * *Allowing the Commonwealth to preference employers with enterprise agreements for procurement and grants, and for other contractual purposes.* > > *Some changes to the FWC’s powers would respond to the Federal Court decision in Coles Supply Chain Pty Ltd v Milford [2020] FCAFC 152 , so that the FWC is no longer required to determine whether a disputed dismissal actually occurred before conferencing or conciliation.* > > *Other changes to the FWC’s powers would mean that the FWC could make vexatious proceeding orders, dismiss a wider range of matters, determine certain matters without hearings, and allow the FWC President to delegate more powers.* > > *Limited exceptions to the prohibition of adverse action, coercion and discrimination under the FW Act would be made to allow the Commonwealth to preference employers with enterprise agreements in procurement, grant, and other contractual activities. This aspect of the Bill has attracted the most stakeholder comment.* > > *At the time of writing, the Bill had not been referred to or reported on by any parliamentary committees.*

Asked how proposed workplace relations legislation could prevent corruption and protect value for money given concerns about enterprise agreements and the CFMEU; the minister said the bill would allow, but not require, preference for genuinely negotiated agreements and announced consultation on a construction code for Commonwealth procurement.

Opposed the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026's procurement provisions, supporting its Fair Work Commission measures on artificial intelligence but arguing union-preference rules could disadvantage small businesses, reduce value for money and repeat problems associated with Queensland's former scheme and alleged CFMEU corruption; the debate was then interrupted.

Moved to suspend standing orders and give precedence to a coalition bill addressing the Fair Work Commission backlog, arguing that the government's bill combined those reforms with procurement, grants, and contracting preferences for businesses linked to union agreements; later moved that the question be put.

Spoke on the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026, supporting reforms to address the Fair Work Commission's workload but opposing provisions that would allow procurement preferences for businesses with union-backed enterprise agreements, arguing they create corruption risks and require separate scrutiny.

Considered the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026 and put opposition, Australian Greens, and Senator David Pocock amendments concerning workplace determinations, less favourable terms, flexibility and consultation provisions, retrospective variations, and a proposed inquiry into corruption risks in Commonwealth procurement and grants before the bill's remaining stages were agreed to.

Argued that allowing Commonwealth supply-chain preferences for businesses with union-backed enterprise agreements could discriminate against comparable businesses. Called for an inquiry into alleged corruption and organised crime involving the construction sector and the CFMEU, stating that failed inquiries had left serious concerns unresolved and that corruption could add 15 to 30 per cent to infrastructure costs.

The bill would permanently enshrine ASIO's compulsory questioning powers in law instead of letting them expire.

It would expand the types of security threats for which an adult can be questioned under a warrant to include sabotage, communal violence promotion, attacks on defence systems, and serious border integrity threats.
People charged with a related offence that is unresolved or imminent could only be questioned before a retired judge serving as a prescribed authority.
Makes the compulsory questioning framework permanent by removing its sunset provision.
Expands the scope of adult compulsory questioning warrants to cover new security threats defined in the ASIO Act.
Amends rules for the appointment and termination of prescribed authorities to strengthen their independence and impartiality.
Adds a new reporting requirement for conduct under a compulsory questioning warrant.
Introduces a safeguard requiring questioning of a person with an unresolved or imminent related charge to happen only before a retired judge.
ASIO, prescribed authorities, people subject to compulsory questioning warrants, and the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

Moved the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand adult questioning warrants to additional security matters, strengthen safeguards and reporting requirements, and permit a further review three years after commencement; debate was adjourned.

Declared that, unless otherwise ordered, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 stood referred to the Federation Chamber after the second-reading debate was adjourned.

Supported the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, arguing that compulsory questioning powers should become permanent, cover additional national security threats and operate with strengthened oversight, reporting and safeguards; noted the powers had been used only 20 times in more than 22 years.

Debated the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, which would make compulsory questioning powers permanent, expand eligible matters and strengthen safeguards and oversight; amendments concerning children were proposed, opposition was stated, and the second-reading question remained unresolved.

Moved bills to make ASIO's compulsory questioning powers permanent and broaden their application while strengthening safeguards and oversight, expand National Immunisation Program access to passive immunological products, and make technical social security and veterans' affairs amendments ahead of 1 July 2026.

Argued that compulsory questioning powers remain important for national security but require strong oversight. Supported expanding the matters covered by warrants, subject to retaining a three-year sunset clause; another speaker opposed making the powers permanent, citing concerns about children, legal representation and extraordinary state powers.

Reaffirmed opposition to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025, reading constituent objections to its expanded compulsory questioning powers and citing concerns from the Law Council and the Australian Human Rights Commission, while renewing calls for a national human rights act; the government proposed amendments adding a sunset clause and a two-year statutory review of the new powers.

As President, put questions on a series of amendments to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2025 from the government, the Australian Greens, the United Australia Party, One Nation and Senator David Pocock, covering sunset dates for questioning powers, judicial preference for prescribed authorities, lawyers' rights during ASIO questioning and repeal of minor (under-18) questioning warrants, before the bill passed its remaining stages.
Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Act (No. 2) 2026
Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026

Argued that the Customs Legislation Amendment (False Trade Marks Infringement Notices) Bill 2026 addresses counterfeit imports through a strict liability offence, financial penalties and Australian Border Force infringement powers, but raised concerns about proportionality, consultation and the absence of a clear trigger, and supported referral to a Senate inquiry.
Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2025

Supported the bill extending ASIO compulsory questioning warrants for 18 months to 7 March 2027. Reported that the extension would prevent disruption while substantive reforms are considered, and supported the bill without amendment while emphasising oversight, accountability and transparency.
Transport Security Amendment (Security of Australia’s Transport Sector) Bill 2025

Supported the Transport Security Amendment (Security of Australia's Transport Sector) Bill 2024 and government amendments, arguing that it would strengthen aviation and maritime security through broader unlawful-interference definitions, mandatory cybersecurity reporting and an all-hazards framework. Sought consultation for 12 months and a 24-month transition period, particularly for regional airports.

Supported the AusCheck Amendment (Global Entry Program) Bill 2025, which would establish Australia's legislative basis for background checks enabling eligible Australians to access expedited immigration and Customs channels in the United States, particularly supporting travel and AUKUS connections.

The Biosecurity Amendment (Strengthening Penalties) Bill 2021 increases maximum civil and criminal penalties for noncompliance with the Biosecurity Act 2015, to deter violations and protect Australia’s $71.2 billion agriculture, fisheries and forestry industries, including fruit growers in areas like Dwellingup and the Perth Hills.
Education Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 2) Bill 2021

The bill ensures resident return visa holders who previously held a permanent humanitarian visa remain eligible for Higher Education Loan Program (HELP) assistance, correcting a drafting oversight, and makes minor amendments to the Education Services for Overseas Students Act to improve the Tuition Protection Service and the Overseas Student Tuition Fund.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019

The member for Canning argued in support of the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, which will trial drug testing of welfare recipients in Mandurah (WA), Logan (Qld) and Canterbury-Bankstown (NSW), claiming the measure is not punitive but aims to help those with drug and alcohol addiction into employment, with 80% of payments quarantined after a first positive test and a $10 million treatment fund available for second-time positive testees.

The speaker argued that the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 is essential to delay, control and risk-manage the return of foreign fighters, and expressed support for the bill in its present form while opposing Labor's amendments. The speaker noted that the parliamentary committee made 18 recommendations, including judicial review (recommendation 7), which the government accepted in principle, and cited an operational imperative to pass the bill.
